newsitem.title: UK: European firms bucked rating uptrend in 1996 - S&P.
newsitem.headline: European firms bucked rating uptrend in 1996 - S&P.

text.p: European companies were subject to more debt rating downgrades than upgrades in the past year, in conflict with the global trend of rising credit ratings, Standard & Poor's (S&P) rating agency said on Monday.
Some 36 issuers were downgraded in Europe in 1996, compared with 26 upgrades, S&P said. On a global basis, the picture was different, with 243 worldwide upgrades and 209 downgrades.

"We anticipate that the moderate growth, low inflation and low interest environment will continue on a global basis," said S&P's George Dallas, managing director of European ratings. "It was very much a positive year."
He said Europe's relatively negative performance did not represent a return to the deterioration of the early 1990s when downgrades were dramatically higher than upgrades.
"Europe was starting from a higher base," said Dallas. "The average rating in Europe is A, whereas the average in the U.S. is BB."
In terms of overall trends, S&P said there had been heightened activity in mergers and acquisitions and in equity-financed transactions.
"Mergers and acquisitions accounted for 16 percent of all rating activity," said Dallas. "That is the highest level since the boom period of 1988."
S&P said the negative trend in European ratings in 1996 reflected more competitive than macroeconomic pressures.
The banking sector, for example, saw more downgrades than upgrades because weak demand for loans and the entrance of non-banks into the financial sector increased the pressure.

"A number of downgrades were the results of consolidation and restructuring," said Dallas. "We expect this trend to continue in 1997 and indeed, it may be accelerated by European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU)."
Upgrades in pharmaceuticals, notably Zeneca and Glaxo Wellcome, were driven by new product development and higher market growth. S&P said it expected consolidation in pharmaceuticals to continue.
S&P noted that demerging and restructuring conglomerates brought downgrades to Hanson Plc and BTR Plc.
"Rapid changes in the media sector may put ratings under pressure in 1997," S&P said.
"Utilities saw a clear negative trend," said Dallas. "Rating actions were less credit driven than event driven."

In the sovereign sector, the picture was bright, with seven upgrades and only one downgrade. S&P said it expected the increased political stability and economic growth in Eastern Europe, which characterised 1996, to continue this year.
